subtitle: The bare-bones way for programs to send each other independent messages over IP.

tldr.problem: Some programs want to send a message to another program with as little protocol machinery as possible, and do not need a reliable ordered stream.
tldr.mechanism: UDP adds an 8-byte header to each message with source and destination ports, a length and a checksum, and sends it as one IP datagram.
tldr.outcome: Delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed, so applications that need ordered, reliable delivery should use TCP instead.

plainLanguage.summary: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) lets one program send a short message to another program over the Internet with very little setup. It is fast and simple, but it does not check that messages arrive or that they arrive in order.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 768 defines the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), a datagram mode of communication that assumes the Internet Protocol (IP) underneath. It lets application programs send messages to other programs with a minimum of protocol mechanism.

The RFC is blunt about the trade-off: the protocol is transaction oriented, and delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed. Applications that need ordered, reliable delivery of streams of data should use TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP sends single messages between programs with as little extra work as possible. It does not guarantee delivery, so programs that need every byte to arrive in order should use TCP instead.

sections.title: The UDP Header
sections.content:
Every UDP message starts with a header of four 16-bit fields: Source Port, Destination Port, Length and Checksum, followed by the data octets. That makes the header 8 bytes.

The source port is optional: when it is not used, a value of zero is inserted. Length counts the header and the data in octets, so its minimum value is eight.

The checksum covers a pseudo header taken from the IP header (the source address, the destination address, the protocol and the UDP length), the UDP header and the data. If the computed checksum is zero it is sent as all ones, and a transmitted checksum of all zeros means the sender did not compute one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with an 8-byte header. It names the sending and receiving ports, gives the message length, and carries a checksum: a number the receiver uses to detect damaged data.

sections.title: Ports, Interfaces and Uses
sections.content:
A user interface should let a program create receive ports, receive data together with the source port and source address, and send a datagram by giving the data, the ports and the addresses. The UDP module must be able to read the source and destination addresses and the protocol field from the IP header.

UDP is protocol number 17 (21 octal) in the Internet Protocol. The RFC names two major uses of the protocol: the Internet Name Server and the Trivial File Transfer protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A program listens on a numbered port. When a message arrives, UDP reads its destination port and passes it to the program listening there.

fields.name: Source Port
fields.desc: Optional; port of the sending process, zero if not used.

fields.name: Destination Port
fields.desc: Port of the receiving process on the destination address.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets in header plus data; the minimum is eight.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum over a pseudo header, the header and the data.

references.text: Postel, J., "Transmission Control Protocol", RFC 761, January 1980.

today: RFC 768 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it is still the definition of UDP.

glossaryTerms.definition: Sorting arriving data to the right receiver, for example by looking at the destination port.
glossaryTerms.plainLanguage: Passing each piece of arriving data to the program it is meant for.
